text.p: Algerians will vote on Thursday to elect deputies for the 380-seat National Assembly, part of a new bicameral parliament being set up after a five-year legislative vacuum.
Under the constitution adopted last November, the National Assembly (lower house) and the Council of the Nation (upper house) form the parliament.
Following are outlines of the powers of the two houses.
Elected by a system of proportional representation. Members serve five-year terms.
Ten days after Thursday's election, the National Assembly starts its maiden session under the presidency of the oldest deputy.
The prime minister, who selects his own cabinet, is appointed, and dismissed, by the Algerian president, not the parliament.
The 380-seat National Assembly can topple the government by rejecting the prime minister's programme. The president can then appoint another head of government.
If the new prime minister fails to win National Assembly approval for his programme, the president dissolves the assembly and calls an election within three months.

Two-thirds of the council's 144 members will be picked by elected local authorities, while the others will be appointed by the president. Elections for the local authorities are to be held by the end of this year but no date has yet been set.
Members of the upper house serve six-year terms.
The head of the Council of the Nation takes over as interim president for 60 days when the head of the state dies, is impeached or incapacitated.

The National Assembly can introduce laws but its proposed legislation must be approved by three-quarters of the Council of the Nation. If the two houses fail to agree on a proposed law, the legislation is withdrawn.
